courses.title: Nǐ hǎo! Chinese
courses.tagline: Every Chinese character started as a little picture — and you can draw them all.
courses.intro: Chinese looks like a wall of tiny drawings, and that is exactly what it is. A person walking. Three mountain peaks. The sun. Once you see the picture inside the character, you cannot un-see it. You will draw them in sand, shout them at your friends, and count goats in Chinese before this course is done.
courses.parentNote: By the end your child will recognise about forty Chinese characters by sight, produce all four tones clearly, and hold a short spoken introduction with a Chinese speaker. Chinese traders, contractors and scholarship programmes are present across the continent, and a child who can greet someone properly in Mandarin is remembered.

modules.title: The Sun, the Mountain and the Walking Person
modules.bigIdea: Chinese characters are not random squiggles — they are pictures that got tidier over three thousand years.

seeThis.caption: On the left the real thing, in the middle the ancient scratched picture, on the right the character people write today.

youNeed: smooth sand, or chalk and a wall
a friend or a younger sibling
doThis: Find smooth sand or a flat wall. Draw a person from behind, walking, with two legs striding. Now rub out the head and the arms. What is left is 人 — rén — person.
Draw three mountain peaks in a row, the middle one tallest. Straighten every line. That is 山 — shān — mountain.
Draw the sun as a circle with a dot in the middle. Now squash the circle into a box. That is 日 — rì — sun.
Draw a tree: one trunk, two branches going up, two roots going down. That is 木 — mù — tree.
Draw all four characters BIG, in a row, and leave them there. Bring someone to look at them and make them guess which is which before you tell them.
Say each one aloud three times while you point at your drawing: rén, shān, rì, mù.
modules.whyItWorks: Your brain stores pictures far better than it stores shapes with no meaning. When you learn 山 as three peaks instead of as three lines, you are attaching the character to something you have seen every day of your life. That link is what stops you forgetting it next week.
modules.challenge: Draw all four characters in the sand, then get a friend to stand in the middle and act out the one you shout. Person? They walk. Sun? They shine.

modules.title: Nǐ hǎo — Say It Loud Enough to Startle a Chicken
modules.bigIdea: Chinese is a language you sing, and the tune changes the meaning, so you must say it out loud and big.

seeThis.visual: mā ˉ  má ˊ  mǎ ˅  mà ˋ
seeThis.caption: Four little roofs above the same letters. Flat, rising, dipping, falling — four different words.

doThis: Stand up. Hold your arm out flat in front of you and sing a long flat 'maaa'. That is tone 1: mā.
Now sweep your arm upward like you are asking a question, and say 'má' going up. That is tone 2.
Dip your arm down and back up like a valley: 'mǎ'. That is tone 3.
Chop your arm down sharply like you are annoyed: 'mà'. That is tone 4.
Now say nǐ hǎo — two dipping tones, two valleys with your arm. Walk up to someone in your compound, wave, and greet them: Nǐ hǎo! Do it to three different people today.
Say xièxie every single time someone hands you anything today. Every time.
modules.whyItWorks: Moving your arm with the tone puts the tune into your body, not just your ears. Learners who drill tones with a hand movement keep the tones years later; learners who only read the tone marks lose them. And greeting real people means the words get attached to real faces.
modules.challenge: Greet someone with Nǐ hǎo and see if you can keep a straight face when they ask what you just said. Then teach them.

modules.title: Counting Goats in Chinese
modules.bigIdea: The first three Chinese numbers are just one, two and three lines — the easiest writing in any language on earth.

seeThis.visual: 一 = 1 line   二 = 2 lines   三 = 3 lines
seeThis.caption: Chinese one, two and three. You already knew how to write them before you started.

youNeed: a cereal box or any stiff card
a charcoal stick, pen or chalk
doThis: Cut your cereal box into ten cards, about the size of your palm.
On the front of each card write one number character: 一 二 三 四 五 六 七 八 九 十. On the back write the Pinyin: yī èr sān sì wǔ liù qī bā jiǔ shí.
Shuffle your cards. Lay them face-down and turn them over one at a time, saying the number aloud before you check the back.
Go outside and count real things in Chinese. Goats. Mangoes on a tree. Bricks in a wall. Say the number out loud each time: yī, èr, sān, sì...
Line the ten cards up in order on the ground and photograph them in your head — or show them to your family and count all the way to shí without looking at the backs.
Keep the cards. You will use them again in module 6.
modules.whyItWorks: Making the flashcards yourself is half the learning — your hand has already written each character before you ever test yourself. And counting real goats instead of counting on a page means the number and the thing arrive in your memory together.
modules.challenge: Count a herd of goats in Chinese out loud while someone else counts them in your own language. Who finishes first?

modules.title: Mother, Horse, Hemp, Scold
modules.bigIdea: Say 'ma' with the wrong tune and you have just called your mother a horse — so today you check your tones against a real voice.

seeThis.visual: 妈 mā 👩  麻 má 🌾  马 mǎ 🐎  骂 mà 😠
seeThis.caption: One sound, four tunes, four completely different words. This is why tones matter.

doThis: Open the course tone drill in the phone's browser. Press play and just listen to mā má mǎ mà three times without speaking.
Now play each one and repeat it straight after, still doing the arm movement you learned in module 2.
Use the record button. Record yourself saying all four, then play yours and the model back to back. Fix the one that sounds furthest off.
Play the mixed-up test: the app plays one 'ma' and you say which of the four it was. Get eight right in a row.
Hand the phone back. For the rest of the day, say 妈妈 with a flat tone every time you speak to or about your mother.
Show one person the four characters and make them hear the difference. If they can hear it, you said it right.
modules.whyItWorks: Your ears must learn the difference before your mouth can produce it, and only a real recorded voice can train them. Recording yourself is the step most learners skip — hearing your own tone next to the model shows you instantly what you cannot hear while you are speaking.
modules.challenge: Say one of the four 'ma' words to a friend with your face hidden. Can they tell you which one you meant?

words.means: question word at the end of a sentence

modules.title: Everybody in the House
modules.bigIdea: Family words are the words you will say most often, and in Chinese most of them are one syllable said twice.

seeThis.visual: 爸爸 bàba  妈妈 māma  哥哥 gēge  姐姐 jiějie
seeThis.caption: See the doubling? The character is written twice and the second one is said light and quick.

doThis: Open the audio list and listen to the five family words. Notice that the second syllable is always softer and shorter.
Repeat each one five times until the light second syllable feels natural rather than forced.
Point at each person in your household as you say their Chinese word aloud. Bàba. Māma. Gēge. Jiějie.
Record yourself saying 我家有五个人 — wǒ jiā yǒu wǔ ge rén — 'there are five people in my family', changing five to your real number.
Draw your family on paper, one stick figure each, and write the Chinese word under each figure. Stick it on the wall.
Teach 妈妈 to your actual mother. She will remember it.
modules.whyItWorks: Words attached to specific real people are stored differently from words on a list — you are not memorising vocabulary, you are renaming people you already love. That is why family words survive long gaps without practice.
modules.challenge: Get your whole family to answer to their Chinese name for one full evening. Anyone who forgets loses a turn at something.

modules.title: Watch the Character Build Itself
modules.bigIdea: Every character is drawn in a fixed order of strokes, and watching that order animate makes the character finally make sense.

seeThis.visual: 口 → 日 → 田 → 中 → 国
seeThis.caption: A mouth, then a sun, then a field, then a line straight through the middle, then a country with treasure inside its walls.

doThis: Open the stroke animation. Watch 口 kǒu draw itself. Left side down, top and right in one stroke, then the bottom line closes the box. Three strokes, always in that order.
Watch 田 tián build. It is a field seen from above, divided into four plots — exactly what farmland looks like from a hill.
Watch 中 zhōng. A box with a line straight through the middle. Middle. China calls itself 中国 — the middle country.
Now put the phone face down and write 口 日 田 中 国 on the back of five new cardboard cards, in the correct stroke order, without peeking.
Turn the phone over and check each one. Fix any stroke you got in the wrong order and write it again.
Hold up your card for 中国 and say Zhōngguó out loud. That is the name of the country on half the goods in your nearest market.
modules.whyItWorks: Stroke order is not fussiness — it is the rhythm that makes characters memorable and readable. Once your hand knows the order, you can write a character you have only seen once, because your hand knows where each line has to start.
modules.challenge: Write 国 on a card and hide it somewhere in the house. Whoever finds it has to say Zhōngguó correctly to win it.

modules.title: Hunt for Chinese in Your Own Market
modules.bigIdea: There is real Chinese writing within walking distance of you, and today you go and read some of it.

seeThis.visual: 中国制造 → 'made in China'
seeThis.caption: Four characters printed on the back of thousands of things sold near you. You can already read two of them.

youNeed: permission to walk to the shop or market with an adult
doThis: Go to a shop, a market stall or your own kitchen shelf. Turn things over and look at the small print on the back.
Find any Chinese characters at all. Torch batteries, phone chargers, plastic basins, slippers, biscuit packets — start there.
Copy three characters you find onto your paper, exactly as they are printed, however hard they look.
Look for 中国 specifically. If you find 中国制造, you have just read 'made in China' — say it out loud: Zhōngguó zhìzào.
Bring your paper home and show someone the characters you copied and the ones you can name.
Add any character you now recognise to your flashcard pile.
modules.whyItWorks: The moment you read real Chinese that was not put there for a learner, the language stops being a school subject and becomes a thing that exists in your world. Learners who find the language in their own street practise far more than learners who only meet it in lessons.
modules.challenge: Challenge an adult to find Chinese writing in the house faster than you. You will win, because you know what you are looking for.

modules.title: Capstone: Your First Real Conversation
modules.bigIdea: Today you stop practising Chinese and simply have a conversation in it, start to finish, with another human being.

seeThis.visual: 你好！→ 你叫什么名字？→ 我叫… → 很高兴认识你！
seeThis.caption: Four lines. That is a whole conversation, and by tonight you will own all four.

youNeed: a friend, sibling or parent willing to play along
the shared phone once, to check your pronunciation
doThis: Learn the four lines in order. Greet, ask the name, give your name, say you are pleased to meet them.
Check each line once against the audio on the phone, then put the phone away for good.
Practise the whole conversation with a sibling, swapping roles so you have said both halves.
Now do it for real, with someone who has not seen you practise. Walk up, greet them with Nǐ hǎo, and run the whole exchange without stopping to translate.
Write your four lines out in characters on a piece of cardboard and hang it where people can see it. This is the certificate you made yourself.
Finish with 再见 — zàijiàn — and mean it.
modules.whyItWorks: A conversation you complete without pausing to translate is the point at which the language leaves your notebook and enters your mouth. Everything before this module was preparation for these four lines, and the four lines will now carry you into every future one.
modules.challenge: Run the full conversation with someone who does not know you are learning Chinese and watch their face on line one.

courses.title: Privet! Russian
courses.tagline: Cyrillic is a secret code, and there are only three kinds of letter to crack.
courses.intro: Russian writing looks like someone wrote English in a mirror during an earthquake. It is not. It is a code with exactly three sorts of letter: friends you already know, tricksters that pretend to be English letters and are not, and brand new shapes nobody can fake. Crack those three groups and you can read Russian words out loud in about a week.
courses.parentNote: Your child will finish able to read Cyrillic aloud, count to ten, and introduce themselves to a Russian speaker with correct stress. Russia offers a large number of engineering and medical scholarships to students across the continent every year, and every one of them begins with reading the alphabet.

modules.title: The Letters That Are Already Your Friends
modules.bigIdea: Some Cyrillic letters look exactly like English letters and sound exactly the same — start there and you get a free head start.

seeThis.visual: К = k   М = m   Т = t   А = a   О = o
seeThis.caption: Five letters that mean what you think they mean. No tricks in this group at all.

youNeed: sand, or chalk and a wall
doThis: Write К М Т А О very large in the sand, far apart. Say each sound as you write it: k, m, t, a, o.
Now build a word. Write К О Т left to right. Read it out: k-o-t. кот. That means cat. You just read Russian.
Build М А М А. Read it out: mama. Yes — it means exactly what it sounds like.
Build Т А М. tam. It means 'there'. Point at something far away and say it: там!
Leave all three words written in the sand and bring someone to look. Read all three aloud to them, pointing letter by letter.
Say кот every time you see a cat today.
modules.whyItWorks: Starting with the letters that transfer for free gives you real reading on day one instead of week three. Reading a whole genuine word out loud in the first ten minutes is what convinces your brain this alphabet is crackable.
modules.challenge: Write кот in the sand and get a sibling to guess what it says. Then point at an actual cat.

modules.title: The Tricksters
modules.bigIdea: Five Cyrillic letters look like English letters and lie to you — learn these five and half of all Russian reading mistakes disappear.

seeThis.visual: Р = r   С = s   Н = n   В = v   У = oo
seeThis.caption: The five liars. P is not p. C is not c. H is not h. B is not b. Y is not y.

doThis: Cut five big cards from the box. On each front write one trickster letter, huge: Р С Н В У.
On the back of each, draw the real sound as a picture clue: Р with a running person, С with a snake, Н with a nose, В with a van, У with a spoon of soup going 'ooo'.
Hold up each card, front first, and say the TRUE sound out loud. Do it ten times fast until the English answer stops jumping out first.
Now read these real words letter by letter: нос (n-o-s, nose), рука (r-u-k-a, hand), вода (v-o-d-a, water). Say each one aloud.
Line all five cards on a wall or a table where the family passes. Ask each person what they think Р says, then correct them. You are now the teacher.
Touch your nose and say нос. Touch your hand and say рука. Drink water and say вода.
modules.whyItWorks: The tricksters are the single biggest cause of slow Cyrillic reading, because your brain fires the English answer before you can stop it. Meeting them as a named group, early and on purpose, replaces that reflex instead of letting it become a habit you fight for years.
modules.challenge: Show a friend the word РОТ and let them read it as 'rot'. Then tell them it says 'rot' meaning mouth — and that they accidentally got it right.

modules.title: The Brand New Shapes
modules.bigIdea: A handful of Cyrillic letters look like nothing you have ever seen, and because of that they are the easiest ones to remember.

seeThis.visual: Ж = zh 🕷️   Ш = sh 🍴   Щ = shch   Ю = yu   Я = ya
seeThis.caption: Ж is a beetle with legs. Ш is a fork with three prongs. Nothing here can trick you, because nothing here pretends.

doThis: Draw Ж really big. It is a beetle with three legs each side. Its sound is the 'zh' in 'measure' or 'treasure'. Buzz it: zhzhzh.
Draw Ш. It is a fork with three prongs, or a bench. Its sound is 'sh'. Now draw Щ — the same fork with a little tail — and say 'shch'.
Draw Я. It is a backwards R and it says 'ya'. It is also a whole word by itself: я means 'I'. Point at your chest and say я.
Draw Ю. It says 'yu'. Write Ю Г — юг — and read it: yug. It means south.
Write ШКОЛА in the sand using your new letters and your old ones. Read it: shkola. School. Then write ЖИРАФ — zhiraf — giraffe.
Bring someone outside, point at your two words, and read them aloud without help.
modules.whyItWorks: Strange shapes stick because your memory has nothing to confuse them with. That is why the letters that look most alarming turn out to be the fastest to learn, and why grouping them separately from the tricksters stops the two problems tangling together.
modules.challenge: Write your own name in Cyrillic in the sand. Sound out every letter. Then write your friend's name and let them approve it.

modules.title: Привет! Hello in Two Sizes
modules.bigIdea: Russian has a small hello for friends and a big hello for adults, and using the wrong one is the first mistake every learner makes.

seeThis.visual: привет 🙋 friends   |   здравствуйте 🤝 adults
seeThis.caption: Short one for your age-mates. Long one for teachers, elders and anybody official.

doThis: Open the audio for the five greeting words and listen to the whole list twice before you say anything.
Say привет after the recording five times. It is easy. pri-VYET, with the punch on the second half.
Now attack здравствуйте. Break it: ZDRA - stvuy - tye. Say it slowly six times, then once at full speed.
Repeat спасибо and пожалуйста until they run smoothly. Note that пожалуйста is said much faster than it is spelled — most Russians say roughly pa-ZHAL-sta.
Record yourself saying all five, play it back, and pick the worst one to fix.
Hand the phone back and greet three people today with привет. Greet one adult with здравствуйте.
modules.whyItWorks: Hearing a real voice is the only way to learn that пожалуйста loses syllables in ordinary speech — no written form can tell you that. Learning the two levels of politeness together also builds the habit of noticing who you are talking to, which is half of speaking any language well.
modules.challenge: Greet your teacher or an elder with здравствуйте tomorrow and keep a straight face when they ask where that came from.

modules.title: Where Is the Punch?
modules.bigIdea: Every Russian word has one syllable you hit harder than the others, and hitting the wrong one is what makes a learner hard to understand.

seeThis.visual: молокó   хорошó   спасѝбо   собáка
seeThis.caption: The little mark shows where the punch lands. Russians do not write it — but they all hear it.

youNeed: a stone or a bottle top to bang with
doThis: Open the audio. Listen to молоко three times and tap the table hard on the syllable that sounds strongest. It is the last one: ma-la-KO.
Do the same for хорошо — kha-ra-SHO — last one again. And собака — sa-BA-ka — middle one.
Now notice the trick: in молоко the first two o's do not sound like 'o' at all, they sound closer to 'a'. That happens because they are not punched. Say it the Russian way: ma-la-KO.
Say each of the five words while banging your stone on the strong syllable. If your bang and the recording's punch land together, you have it.
Record yourself saying all five words and compare. Fix any word where your punch is in the wrong place.
Say хорошо out loud when anyone asks how you are today. It means 'good'.
modules.whyItWorks: Russian vowels change their sound depending on whether they are stressed, so stress is not decoration — it is part of the pronunciation. Tapping the beat physically is what moves stress from something you know into something you do without thinking.
modules.challenge: Say ma-la-KO and MO-lo-ko to a friend and ask which sounds more Russian. Then tell them why.

modules.title: Counting Mangoes to Ten
modules.bigIdea: Ten Russian numbers, learned as a chant, will carry you through prices, ages, dates and phone numbers for the rest of your life.

seeThis.visual: 1 один · 2 два · 3 три · 4 четыре · 5 пять
seeThis.caption: три really does mean three. Some words travelled a very long way and barely changed.

youNeed: ten small things — stones, seeds, mango pips
doThis: Listen to the numbers one to ten straight through, twice, without repeating.
Now repeat after the audio, laying down one stone for each number as you say it.
Notice три — tri — three. It sounds like 'three' because both words come from the same ancient root. So does два — dva — two.
Cover the screen and count your ten stones out loud from memory. If you stumble, uncover and fix just that number.
Count real things all day: mangoes, goats, chairs, people on a bench. Out loud, in Russian.
Show a family member your ten stones and count them in Russian while they watch.
modules.whyItWorks: Numbers are the highest-value words in any language because you use them daily and can practise them on anything in sight. Laying down a stone per number turns the chant into something your hands remember as well as your mouth.
modules.challenge: Count to десять in Russian faster than your sibling can count to ten in English. Practise first — this is winnable.

modules.title: Read a Real Russian Word in the Wild
modules.bigIdea: Cyrillic turns up on machinery, medicine boxes and signs — and now that you can read it, you cannot walk past it.

seeThis.visual: ВХОД ⬅️ in   ВЫХОД ➡️ out
seeThis.caption: Two words that differ by one letter. Ы is the difference between coming in and going out.

youNeed: permission to look around the house, workshop or shop with an adult
doThis: Learn the five sign words first: вход, выход, стоп, открыто, закрыто. Read each one aloud letter by letter.
Now go and look. Check generator plates, water pumps, welding gear, old tools, medicine packets and tyre markings for Cyrillic writing.
Copy any Cyrillic you find onto your paper exactly as written, even if you have no idea what it says.
Sound out every word you copied, letter by letter, out loud. You do not need to know the meaning — reading it is the win.
Write вход and выход on two pieces of card and tape them to the correct sides of your door. Leave them up.
Show one adult your signs and read them the difference between the two words.
modules.whyItWorks: Decoding writing that was never meant for a learner proves the alphabet is genuinely yours. And two words that differ by a single letter force you to read carefully rather than guessing from the shape — the exact habit that makes a fluent reader.
modules.challenge: Find one piece of Cyrillic writing somewhere near you that nobody else in your household can read. Then read it to them.

modules.title: Capstone: Meet Me, in Russian
modules.bigIdea: Today you introduce yourself to another person in Russian, from hello to goodbye, with nothing written in front of you.

seeThis.visual: Привет! → Как тебя зовут? → Меня зовут… → Очень приятно!
seeThis.caption: Four lines, and the whole introduction is done. Russians really do say exactly this.

youNeed: the phone once, to check the audio
doThis: Learn the four lines. Meня зовут literally means 'they call me' — Russian does not say 'my name is'.
Check the pronunciation once on the phone, especially зовут — za-VOOT, punch on the second half. Then put the phone away.
Practise both halves with a sibling, swapping roles so you have asked as well as answered.
Now do it for real with somebody who has not watched you practise. Greet them, ask their name, give yours, say очень приятно.
Write the four lines out in Cyrillic on cardboard, by hand, and hang it up. Every letter on that card is one you can now read.
Finish with до свидания. You have had a conversation in Russian.
modules.whyItWorks: An introduction is the one conversation you will repeat for the rest of your life in this language, so it is the right thing to own completely. Doing it once, live, without a script, is what turns four memorised lines into something you can actually use.
modules.challenge: Introduce yourself in Russian to somebody who has no idea you were learning it, and see how long it takes them to ask a question.

courses.title: Marhaba! Arabic
courses.tagline: Arabic letters hold hands, and some of them are the same shape wearing different dots.
courses.intro: Arabic runs right to left, and its letters join up like people holding hands in a line. Even better: many letters are the SAME shape, and only the dots tell them apart. Learn one shape and you get three letters free. You will be writing your own name in Arabic much sooner than you think.
courses.parentNote: Your child will finish able to write and recognise a solid group of Arabic letters in their joined forms, greet and reply in Arabic, count to ten, and read simple words on real packaging. Arabic is spoken right across North Africa, the Sahel and the Horn, is a working language of the African Union, and is the language of the Qur'an for families where that matters.

modules.title: One Shape, Three Letters, Just Dots
modules.bigIdea: ب ت ث are the same little boat — only the dots change — so you learn three letters for the price of one.

seeThis.visual: ب  ت  ث   🛶
seeThis.caption: One boat. One dot below is b. Two dots above is t. Three dots above is th.

youNeed: smooth sand, or chalk and a wall
doThis: Draw a wide shallow boat in the sand — a smooth curve with a small tail on the right. That is the shape all three letters share.
Put ONE dot underneath it. That is ب — the sound b. Say it: baa.
Wipe the dot. Now put TWO dots on top. That is ت — the sound t. Say it: taa.
Wipe again. Put THREE dots on top. That is ث — the sound 'th' as in 'think'. Say it: thaa.
Draw all three boats in a row and leave them. Bring someone over and make them tell you which is which just from the dots.
Now remember which direction Arabic runs. Stand at the RIGHT edge of your sand and write towards the LEFT. Do it three times so your arm learns it.
modules.whyItWorks: Arabic has twenty-eight letters, but far fewer basic shapes — the dots do a huge amount of the work. Learning by shape family instead of by alphabet order means you meet each new shape only once, which is one of the genuinely fastest ways into the script.
modules.challenge: Draw a boat with no dots and dare a friend to add dots to make the letter you shout. Three rounds each.

modules.title: Letters Hold Hands
modules.bigIdea: Arabic letters change shape depending on whether they are at the start, the middle or the end of a word — because they are joining onto their neighbours.

seeThis.visual: ب + ي + ت  →  بيت
seeThis.caption: Three separate letters on the left. On the right they have joined hands and become one word: house.

doThis: Cut three cardboard strips. Write ب on one, ي on the next, ت on the last, one letter per strip.
Lay them out RIGHT to LEFT in that order. Now push them together until they touch. That squashing together is exactly what Arabic writing does.
Copy the joined word بيت onto one new card. Notice how the boat at the start lost its tail — it gave up its tail to hold the next letter's hand.
Write بيت big on your wall or in the sand and say bayt. Then point at your actual house.
Do the same trick with شمس — shams — sun, and قمر — qamar — moon. Copy them joined.
Hold up your three word-cards and read them aloud to someone, right to left, pointing as you go.
modules.whyItWorks: Beginners often learn the isolated letters and then panic at real Arabic, because real Arabic is always joined. Meeting the joining on day two — physically pushing cards together — means you never build the wrong mental picture in the first place.
modules.challenge: Make cards for the letters in your friend's name and let them push the cards together into a joined word.

modules.title: Peace Be Upon You
modules.bigIdea: The Arabic greeting is a whole sentence with a fixed reply, and knowing the reply is what makes you sound like you belong.

seeThis.visual: السلام عليكم 🫱 → 🫲 وعليكم السلام
seeThis.caption: You say 'peace be upon you'. They say 'and upon you, peace'. The words come back to you reversed.

doThis: Say مرحبا — marḥaban — out loud ten times. It simply means hello and works anywhere.
Now learn the big one: السلام عليكم — as-salāmu ʿalaykum. Break it into three: as-sa-LAAM · a-LAY-kum. Say each part, then join them.
Learn the reply: وعليكم السلام — wa ʿalaykumu s-salām. Practise both halves with a sibling, one saying and one answering.
Say شكرا — shukran — thank you — every time someone hands you something today. Count how many times. Aim for ten.
Write مرحبا big in the sand or on cardboard and leave it where people walk past.
Greet three real people in Arabic today and give the correct reply if anyone greets you back.
modules.whyItWorks: Greetings in Arabic are call-and-response, so learning only your half leaves you stuck the moment someone answers. Practising both sides means you can keep an exchange going instead of freezing, which is what turns a memorised phrase into a real skill.
modules.challenge: Greet someone with السلام عليكم and see whether they give you the right answer back. Teach them if they do not.

modules.title: The Sounds From Deeper Down
modules.bigIdea: Arabic has sounds made further back in the throat than any English sound, and you need a real voice in your ear to find them.

seeThis.visual: ع 😮  ح 😤  خ 😾  ق 🗣️
seeThis.caption: Four sounds English does not have. All of them live behind your tongue, not in front of it.

doThis: Open the sound drill. Listen to ع, ح, خ and ق three times each with your eyes closed before you attempt any of them.
Put your hand flat on your throat. Say ح — a strong breathy h, like fogging up glass but harder. You should feel it tighten under your hand.
Now خ — the scratchy sound at the back, like gargling gently. Then ق — a k made as far back as your throat will let you.
ع is the hardest. Listen five times, then squeeze your throat slightly and make a low 'a'. Do not worry about perfect. Worry about trying.
Record yourself saying عين, حليب, خبز and قلم. Play your recording next to the model and pick the closest and the furthest.
Put the phone down and say حليب out loud next to real milk, and خبز next to real bread.
modules.whyItWorks: These four sounds cannot be learned from writing, because there is nothing in English to compare them to — only a recorded voice can show you the target. Feeling the sound with your hand on your throat gives you physical feedback, so you know when you have found the right place and not just the right idea.
modules.challenge: Make the خ sound at a friend and see if they can copy it. Then teach them the throat trick.

modules.title: Everyone in the Family
modules.bigIdea: Arabic family words are short, ancient and used constantly — and two of them sound almost like baby words in every language on earth.

seeThis.visual: أب 👨  أم 👩  أخ 👦  أخت 👧
seeThis.caption: Father, mother, brother, sister. Notice that sister is just brother wearing an extra letter.

doThis: Listen to the six family words. Notice that أخت — ukht — sister — is أخ — akh — brother — with a ت added on the end. That ت ending marks the feminine in Arabic again and again.
Repeat each word after the recording five times.
Point at each real person in your home and say their Arabic word aloud as you point.
Draw your family on paper and write the Arabic word under each figure, right to left, joined up.
Say أسرتي — usratī — 'my family' — while you show your drawing to somebody. Stick the drawing on the wall.
Test yourself: put the phone away, look at your drawing, and name everybody in Arabic without help.
modules.whyItWorks: Spotting that ت turns brother into sister is your first piece of Arabic grammar, and it arrives disguised as vocabulary. Patterns learned that way — noticed rather than taught — are the ones learners keep.
modules.challenge: Ask your family to answer only to their Arabic name at supper. Anyone who forgets clears the plates.

modules.title: Counting to Ten at the Stall
modules.bigIdea: Arabic numbers are the words you will hear first at any market from Nouakchott to Khartoum, so learn them by ear before you meet them on paper.

seeThis.visual: ١ ٢ ٣ ٤ ٥  ·  واحد اثنان ثلاثة أربعة خمسة
seeThis.caption: The digits on top are Arabic-Indic numerals — used on price tags across North Africa and the Sahel.

youNeed: ten stones, seeds or bottle tops
doThis: Listen to one to ten straight through twice. Do not repeat yet — just hear the rhythm.
Now repeat after the audio, placing one stone for each number.
Notice that ثلاثة — thalātha — three — uses the three-dot letter ث you learned in module 1. You can already read the first letter of it.
Cover the screen and count your stones aloud in Arabic from memory.
Copy the Arabic-Indic digits ١ ٢ ٣ ٤ ٥ onto a card. If you see these on a price tag, you can now read the price.
Count real things aloud in Arabic today: mangoes, oranges, coins, goats. Out loud, where people can hear you.
modules.whyItWorks: Numbers are the fastest-paying words in any language because you can practise them on anything you can see. Learning the spoken numbers and the written digits together also means a price tag becomes readable, not just hearable.
modules.challenge: Ask an adult the price of something, then count that number out loud in Arabic before they can say it in your own language.

modules.title: Read the Packet in Your Own Kitchen
modules.bigIdea: Arabic is printed on food, soap and medicine sold all over the continent — go and read some of it today.

seeThis.visual: حليب · سكر · ملح · أرز · زيت
seeThis.caption: Milk, sugar, salt, rice, oil. Five words that appear on real packaging in kitchens everywhere.

youNeed: your kitchen shelf, or a shop with an adult
doThis: Learn the five words first. Read each one aloud, right to left, letter by letter.
Now go to your kitchen shelf or a nearby shop. Turn packets around and look for Arabic script — dates, tinned goods, oil bottles, tea, soap and medicine boxes are the best hunting grounds.
Copy any Arabic writing you find onto your paper, exactly as printed, joined up.
Sound out at least one word you copied. You do not need the meaning — reading it aloud is the achievement.
Label five real things in your kitchen with cards in Arabic: حليب, سكر, ملح, أرز, زيت. Tape them on and leave them.
Walk one family member around the kitchen and read your labels to them.
modules.whyItWorks: Reading Arabic that was printed for shoppers rather than for learners is the moment the script becomes real. Labelling things in your own home also gives you dozens of small unplanned reviews every day, without any effort at all.
modules.challenge: Find one packet in the house with Arabic on it that nobody else in your family had noticed. Then read it to them.

modules.title: Capstone: A Real Arabic Conversation
modules.bigIdea: Today you greet, ask, answer and part — a complete conversation in Arabic, with a real person, out loud.

seeThis.visual: مرحبا → ما اسمك؟ → اسمي… → كيف حالك؟ → بخير، شكرا
seeThis.caption: Read it right to left. Five lines and the conversation is complete.

youNeed: the phone once, to check pronunciation
doThis: Learn the five lines in order. اسمي — ismī — literally means 'my name'.
Check them once against the audio, paying attention to the ح in كيف حالك. Then put the phone away.
Practise both roles with a sibling until neither of you has to stop and think.
Now have the conversation for real, with somebody who has not watched you rehearse. Start with مرحبا and do not switch languages until you reach مع السلامة.
Write the whole conversation out in Arabic script on cardboard, joined up, right to left. Hang it on the wall.
Point at your cardboard and read the whole thing aloud to your family. That is the proof.
modules.whyItWorks: Running a full exchange without pausing to translate is the step that converts memorised phrases into usable language. And writing it out joined, right to left, proves that the script you met as strange dots eight modules ago now belongs to your own hand.
modules.challenge: Have the whole conversation with somebody who actually speaks Arabic. Ask them to correct exactly one thing.

courses.title: Chinese for Teens
courses.tagline: Learn the system behind the characters and you stop memorising and start reading.
courses.intro: Nobody memorises fifty thousand Chinese characters. They learn a few hundred building blocks and then see those blocks inside everything else. This course gives you the blocks, the tones, the market vocabulary and the scholarship vocabulary — and finishes with you introducing yourself properly to a Chinese speaker.
courses.parentNote: Your teenager will finish able to read and write around sixty characters, distinguish the tones and the difficult zh/ch/sh consonants, handle basic price negotiation vocabulary, and deliver a competent spoken self-introduction. Chinese-language ability is a real differentiator for trade apprenticeships, contracting work and the Chinese government scholarship programmes that recruit across the continent every year.

modules.title: Blocks, Not Characters
modules.bigIdea: Complicated characters are simple characters stacked together, and once you see the stacking you never look at a character the same way again.

seeThis.visual: 木 tree → 林 woods → 森 forest
seeThis.caption: One tree. Two trees. Three trees. The character for forest is literally a small forest.

youNeed: chalk and a wall, or sand and a stick
doThis: Write 木 mù — tree — large. One trunk, one crossbar, two legs spreading like roots.
Now write it twice side by side: 林 lín. That means woods. Write it three times stacked: 森 sēn. Forest.
Do the same with fire. Write 火 huǒ — a flame with sparks either side. Then double it: 炎 yán, a blaze.
Write 人 rén — person — then put a roof over three of them. Look at 众 zhòng: three people together, meaning 'crowd'.
Write all six characters in a row on your wall and draw arrows showing which simple block builds which complex one. Leave the diagram up.
Explain your diagram out loud to one person. If they can follow it, you have understood it.
modules.whyItWorks: Chinese characters are a combining system, not a list. Once you learn to decompose a character into its parts, an unfamiliar character stops being noise and becomes a puzzle with visible pieces — which is exactly how literate Chinese readers handle characters they have not met before.
modules.challenge: Show someone 木, 林 and 森 without saying anything and see if they can guess the meanings in order. Most people can.

modules.title: Buy or Sell — One Stroke Apart
modules.bigIdea: Tones are not an accent, they are part of the word, and two words can differ only by their tone and mean opposite things.

seeThis.visual: 买 mǎi = buy    卖 mài = sell
seeThis.caption: Nearly the same character, opposite meanings, and the tone is what your listener hears first.

doThis: Write 买 mǎi and 卖 mài on cardboard, very large, one on each side. Note that 卖 has an extra stroke on top — the seller has something on their head to carry to market.
Above each character draw the tone shape as a line: a dipping valley for mǎi, a steep drop for mài.
Say each ten times with a matching hand movement. Dip for third tone, chop down for fourth.
Do the same with 水 shuǐ (water) and 睡 shuì (sleep). Write both, mark both tone lines, say both twenty times.
Hold up a card at random and have a partner say the word with the correct tone. Swap. Ten rounds each.
Leave both cardboard sheets on the wall where you sit. You will glance at them a hundred times this week.
modules.whyItWorks: Drawing the tone as a line above the character binds the pitch to the word visually, so you cannot store the word without the tone. Learners who file tones separately from vocabulary end up with a large vocabulary nobody can understand.
modules.challenge: Say mǎi or mài to a partner with your back turned and see whether they can tell buying from selling.

modules.title: How Much Is That, Really
modules.bigIdea: Price vocabulary is the most immediately useful Chinese you can own, because the first Chinese speaker you meet may well be selling something.

seeThis.visual: 多少钱？ = how + few + money = 'how much money?'
seeThis.caption: Chinese builds the question out of three plain words. Once you see the parts, you never forget the phrase.

youNeed: a friend to play the trader
doThis: Write each of the five words on its own card, character on the front, Pinyin and meaning on the back.
Learn 多少钱 duōshao qián as one unit, not three words. Say it twenty times until it is a single sound.
Set up a market game. Your friend lays out five real objects and plays the trader. You point and ask 多少钱?
They answer with a number in Chinese. You reply either 太贵了 — tài guì le — too expensive — or 好，我买 — hǎo, wǒ mǎi — good, I'll buy.
Swap roles and run it again. Make the prices ridiculous so you have to use 太贵了 often.
Write out the whole exchange on cardboard as a script and hang it up.
modules.whyItWorks: Role-play with real objects forces you to produce language under a small amount of pressure, which is what makes it available later. And the phrase 多少钱 is high frequency — the words you will use most are the ones worth over-practising.
modules.challenge: Run the market game with a sibling who does not speak Chinese and teach them their lines as you go.

modules.title: zh ch sh Against z c s
modules.bigIdea: Six consonants split into two families, and getting them apart is the difference between being understood and being asked to repeat yourself.

seeThis.visual: zh ch sh 👅⬆️  |  z c s 👅➡️
seeThis.caption: Curled tongue up behind the ridge for the first three. Flat tongue behind the teeth for the second three.

doThis: Listen to the pair 四 sì and 十 shí ten times before you speak. This is the classic pair Chinese learners confuse.
Curl your tongue tip up towards the roof of your mouth, just behind the ridge, and say shí. Now flatten your tongue behind your teeth and say sì.
Do the same for 中 zhōng against 走 zǒu, and 吃 chī against 次 cì.
Record yourself saying 四十 sìshí — forty. This one word contains both families and is the hardest test.
Play your recording next to the model. If your 四 and your 十 sound identical, curl harder on the second one and record again.
Get eight out of ten right on the mixed listening test before you stop.
modules.whyItWorks: These two consonant families are the most common cause of a learner being misunderstood, and they cannot be fixed by reading — only by listening and by feeling where your tongue sits. Recording yourself is essential here because the difference is inaudible to you while you are producing it.
modules.challenge: Say 四十 to a friend and ask them to write down whether they heard 'sss' or 'shh' first. See if you can control it.

modules.title: The Scholarship Words
modules.bigIdea: There are real Chinese government scholarships open to students across the continent, and the vocabulary that surrounds them is small enough to learn in one sitting.

seeThis.visual: 学 xué = to study → 学生 student · 学校 school · 大学 university
seeThis.caption: One character, 学, sits inside all of them. Learn it once and read four words.

doThis: Listen to the five words and notice how many contain 学 xué. Circle that character every time you write it.
Repeat each word after the audio five times, keeping the tones sharp — 老师 lǎoshī has a dip then a flat, and learners flatten both.
Write 奖学金 jiǎngxuéjīn — scholarship — ten times by hand. It is three characters: prize, study, gold.
Record yourself saying 我是学生 — wǒ shì xuéshēng — 'I am a student' — and compare it to the model.
Write out 我在学中文 — wǒ zài xué Zhōngwén — 'I am studying Chinese' — on cardboard and put it above your desk or your sleeping place.
Say that sentence out loud to one adult and explain what it means.
modules.whyItWorks: Learning vocabulary in families around a shared character means every new word reinforces an old one instead of competing with it. And knowing the exact words used on scholarship pages means that when you meet those pages, you already recognise what you are looking at.
modules.challenge: Find out whether any student from your area has studied in China. Ask what language level they needed.

modules.title: Typing Chinese With a Phone Keyboard
modules.bigIdea: You type Chinese by typing Pinyin and choosing the character — which means your Pinyin and your tones are what unlock the writing.

seeThis.visual: type 'shouji' → 手机 · 收集 · 首级 → pick 手机
seeThis.caption: The keyboard offers you every character that matches the sound. You have to recognise the right one.

youNeed: permission to add a keyboard, or the course's browser typing pad
doThis: Open the typing pad in the browser. Type 'nihao' and watch 你好 appear in the options. Select it.
Type 'shouji' and look at the list of candidates. Several different words share that sound. Find 手机 — mobile phone — and choose it.
Type each of the five words of this module by their Pinyin and select the correct character from the list every time.
Now type your own name in Chinese if you know it, or type 我是学生 as a full sentence.
Write down on paper which words the keyboard offered you that were NOT the one you wanted. That list is your homework — those are words that sound identical to ones you know.
Show one person the sentence you typed on the screen and read it aloud to them.
modules.whyItWorks: Pinyin input is how almost every Chinese person actually writes on a device, and it flips the skill you need: you must recognise characters rather than produce every stroke. Practising recognition against a list of similar-sounding options is one of the fastest ways to sharpen it.
modules.challenge: Type a short message in Chinese and show it to someone. Have them ask you what each character means.

modules.title: Read the Signs and the Shipping Marks
modules.bigIdea: Chinese appears on containers, packaging and equipment near you, and the handful of characters used on signs is a short, closed list.

seeThis.visual: 出口 = out + mouth = exit / export
seeThis.caption: The same two characters mean 'exit' on a door and 'export' on a shipping crate. One idea, two uses.

youNeed: permission to walk to a market, port road, workshop or shop with an adult
doThis: Learn the five sign characters first and write each one three times by hand.
Notice 出口 chūkǒu and 入口 rùkǒu. 出 is going out, 入 is going in, and 口 is a mouth or opening. Exit and entrance.
Go out and hunt. Look at packing crates, equipment plates, tool boxes, electronics, tyres and imported goods for Chinese characters.
Copy at least five characters you find. Circle any you already know.
Look specifically for 小心 xiǎoxīn — 'be careful' — printed as a warning. If you find it, you have read a real safety instruction in Chinese.
Bring your paper home and read your finds aloud to one person.
modules.whyItWorks: Sign Chinese is a small, high-frequency vocabulary that repeats endlessly, which makes it the best possible reading practice for a beginner. Finding it yourself, in your own street, is also what proves the language is not confined to a lesson.
modules.challenge: Photograph or copy one piece of Chinese writing nobody around you can read, then translate it for them.

modules.title: Capstone: Introduce Yourself Like You Mean It
modules.bigIdea: Today you deliver a real spoken self-introduction in Chinese — the exact thing asked for at a scholarship interview or a first meeting with a Chinese trader.

seeThis.visual: 你好，我叫… 我来自… 我在学中文。很高兴认识你。
seeThis.caption: Four sentences. This is a complete, genuine introduction that a Chinese speaker will recognise instantly.

youNeed: a partner to receive the introduction
the phone once, to check your tones
doThis: Write out your own version of the four sentences, filling in your name and where you are from.
Check every tone once against the audio, especially 很高兴认识你. Then put the phone away.
Say the whole introduction out loud five times standing up, without notes.
Now deliver it to a real person, face to face, with a handshake and eye contact. Do not stop and translate in the middle. If you stumble, keep going.
Write the whole introduction out in characters on cardboard and hang it where you sleep. This is what you have built.
Ask your listener one question afterwards: 请问，你叫什么名字？ — and understand the answer.
modules.whyItWorks: A self-introduction is the highest-return piece of language in any course, because it is the only speech you will give again and again for years. Delivering it once, standing, to a live person, is what makes it available under pressure later.
modules.challenge: Deliver the introduction to somebody who actually speaks Mandarin and ask them for one correction. Just one.

courses.title: Russian for Teens
courses.tagline: Crack Cyrillic in a week, then go after the vocabulary that opens laboratories.
courses.intro: Cyrillic takes about a week if you attack it in the right order — the friendly letters, the liars, then the strange shapes. After that Russian rewards you fast, because thousands of scientific and technical words came into Russian from the same roots as English. This course takes you from zero to introducing yourself, reading real technical labels, and saying why you want to study.
courses.parentNote: Your teenager will finish able to read Cyrillic fluently aloud, handle greetings and basic requests with correct stress, read technical and safety labelling, and give a spoken self-introduction suitable for a scholarship interview. Russian universities admit substantial numbers of African students each year in medicine and engineering, and language preparation is a formal part of that route.

modules.title: The Words You Can Already Read
modules.bigIdea: Hundreds of Russian words are borrowed from the same international vocabulary as English, so your first real reading is easier than it looks.

seeThis.visual: СПОРТ · ФУТБОЛ · БАНК · МЕТРО · ТЕЛЕФОН
seeThis.caption: Sound out each one letter by letter and you will hear a word you already know.

youNeed: chalk and a wall, or sand and a stick
doThis: Write the alphabet key you need first: А=a Б=b В=v Г=g Д=d Е=ye К=k Л=l М=m Н=n О=o П=p Р=r С=s Т=t У=oo Ф=f.
Now write СПОРТ. Decode it letter by letter using your key: s-p-o-r-t. Say it aloud. You just read Russian.
Decode ФУТБОЛ. f-oo-t-b-o-l. Football. Decode БАНК, МЕТРО and ТЕЛЕФОН the same way, out loud, one letter at a time.
Write all five words large on your wall in Cyrillic with nothing else — no translation.
Bring somebody to your wall and make them decode one word with your help. Watching the moment it clicks for them will lock it in for you.
Write three more international words yourself in Cyrillic: ДОКТОР, ТАКСИ, РАДИО. Read them aloud.
modules.whyItWorks: Reading real words on day one is what stops the alphabet feeling like a wall. Borrowed vocabulary lets you practise decoding without the extra load of learning meanings, so all your effort goes into the letters themselves.
modules.challenge: Write ФУТБОЛ on a wall or a ball and see how long it takes a friend to work it out with no clues.

modules.title: The Five Letters That Lie to You
modules.bigIdea: Р С Н В У look like Latin letters and are not, and until you kill that reflex your reading will stay slow.

seeThis.visual: Р=r  С=s  Н=n  В=v  У=oo
seeThis.caption: Every one of these has a Latin twin with a different sound. These five cause most beginner errors.

youNeed: a partner with a watch or a counting voice
doThis: Cut five cards and write one liar letter on each, large.
Have your partner hold them up one at a time, fast, while you call the correct sound. Any hesitation counts as a miss.
Run it until you get twenty in a row with no hesitation. Speed is the whole point — you are overwriting a reflex, not learning a fact.
Now decode these five real words letter by letter: ресторан, доктор, студент, университет, инженер.
Notice what happened: every one of them is an international word, and all five contain a liar letter. That is why they look unreadable until the liars are fixed.
Write ИНЖЕНЕР — engineer — on cardboard and put it on your wall. That is one of the reasons this language is worth your time.
modules.whyItWorks: Latin-lookalike letters are the single biggest bottleneck in Cyrillic reading, because your brain answers before you can intervene. Drilling them under time pressure, as a named group, is what replaces the wrong automatic answer with the right one instead of leaving both competing.
modules.challenge: Time yourself reading all five words aloud. Then beat your own time twice.

modules.title: The Shapes With No Twin
modules.bigIdea: Ж Ш Щ Ц Ч Э look like nothing else on earth, which makes them the last hurdle and the easiest one.

seeThis.visual: Ж zh · Ш sh · Щ shch · Ц ts · Ч ch · Э e
seeThis.caption: Six letters with no Latin lookalike at all. Nothing here can trick you.

youNeed: sand or chalk for the big versions
doThis: Write each of the six letters huge in the sand and say its sound as you write it. Ж buzzes. Ш hisses. Ч is 'ch' as in 'church'. Ц is the 'ts' at the end of 'cats'.
Look at Ш and Щ side by side. The only difference is the little tail. Ш is 'sh', Щ is a longer, softer 'shch'.
Now decode the five words of this module letter by letter, out loud, slowly.
The hard one is женщина — zhen-shchi-na — woman. It contains both Ж and Щ. Write it five times by hand.
Make six cards, one per letter, and get somebody to hold them up at random while you call the sounds. Twenty correct in a row.
Write чай — chay — tea — on a card and stick it on the kettle or the tea tin. You will read it every day.
modules.whyItWorks: Unfamiliar shapes have no competing memory attached to them, so they stick faster than the lookalikes ever will. Handling them as their own group means the genuinely hard problem — the liars — gets the attention it deserves rather than being diluted.
modules.challenge: Write женщина and dare anyone in the house to pronounce it. Then do it yourself, correctly, and enjoy it.

modules.title: Stress, and Why Your O Turns Into an A
modules.bigIdea: Unstressed Russian vowels change their sound, so pronouncing every letter as written is the fastest way to sound wrong.

seeThis.visual: молоко → written m-o-l-o-k-o → said ma-la-KÓ
seeThis.caption: Three o's on paper. Only the last one is actually pronounced as an o.

doThis: Listen to молоко five times without speaking. Write down where you hear the strongest syllable.
Now say it the Russian way: ma-la-KÓ. Both unstressed o's soften towards a. Say it fifteen times.
Do the same with хорошо — kha-ra-SHÓ — and Москва — ma-SKVÁ. Same rule, every time.
Now do спасибо — spa-SÍ-ba. The stress is in the middle and the final o softens to a. Almost every learner says spa-si-BO and it is wrong.
Record yourself saying all five words. Compare each against the model and mark which ones have the stress in the wrong place.
Fix the worst one, re-record it, and only stop when the beat lands in the same place as the model.
modules.whyItWorks: Vowel reduction is a rule, not an accident, and once you know the rule you can pronounce new words correctly on sight as long as you know where the stress falls. Learners who never meet this rule keep a heavy foreign accent no matter how much vocabulary they add.
modules.challenge: Say spa-si-BO and spa-SI-ba to a friend and ask which sounds Russian. Then explain the rule to them.

modules.title: The Laboratory and the Hospital
modules.bigIdea: The Russian words for medicine and science are the reason many students learn this language at all, and they are unusually easy to recognise.

seeThis.visual: физика · химия · биология · наука
seeThis.caption: Physics, chemistry, biology, science. Three of these four you could have guessed.

doThis: Listen to the five words and repeat each five times, watching your stress placement from module 4.
Notice that физика, химия and биология are all borrowed international words, so you get them nearly free. наука — science — and врач — doctor — are genuinely Russian and must be learned properly.
врач is the hard one. There is no international cousin to help you. Write it fifteen times by hand and say it every time.
Record yourself saying я хочу быть врачом — ya khochu byt' vrachom — 'I want to be a doctor' — and check it against the model.
Write that sentence out in Cyrillic on cardboard, substituting инженером (engineer) if that is closer to the truth for you.
Put the cardboard where you study. Read it aloud once a day.
modules.whyItWorks: Separating the free borrowed words from the ones that must be memorised lets you spend your effort where it is actually needed. And attaching the vocabulary to a real ambition — the thing you want to be — makes it something you rehearse rather than revise.
modules.challenge: Find out what a Russian medical or engineering degree requires in language level. Then say your sentence out loud to one adult.

modules.title: Five Sentences That Get You Out of Trouble
modules.bigIdea: A handful of first-person verb phrases will carry you through most of a real conversation long before you understand any grammar.

seeThis.visual: я знаю · я не знаю · я хочу · я могу · помогите!
seeThis.caption: I know. I don't know. I want. I can. Help. Notice that 'not' is just не placed in front.

doThis: Listen and repeat each of the five phrases five times.
Notice the pattern: to make anything negative you simply put не in front of the verb. я знаю becomes я не знаю. That is the whole rule.
Build your own negatives out loud: я не хочу, я не могу. You just made new sentences from a rule instead of memorising them.
Record yourself saying all five plus your two new negatives, and check the stress on хочу — kha-CHÚ — punch on the second half.
Play a game with a partner: they ask you anything at all and you must answer only with one of your seven phrases. Ten questions.
Write the seven phrases on cardboard in Cyrillic and hang them where you can see them.
modules.whyItWorks: Learning one productive rule — не goes in front — gives you more sentences than memorising ten fixed phrases would. This is the first point in the course where you generate Russian you were never taught, which is what learning a language actually consists of.
modules.challenge: Answer a whole conversation with a friend using only these seven phrases and see how far you get.

modules.title: Read the Machine
modules.bigIdea: Russian-made and Russian-labelled equipment turns up in workshops, clinics and generators, and safety words are the first real Russian most engineers read.

seeThis.visual: ВКЛ ⏻ on   ВЫКЛ ⭘ off   ОПАСНО ⚠️
seeThis.caption: ВКЛ and ВЫКЛ are the abbreviations printed on real switches. ОПАСНО means danger.

youNeed: permission to look at equipment with an adult
doThis: Learn the five words first and read each one aloud, letter by letter.
Note the shortcuts: включить is often printed just as ВКЛ, and выключить as ВЫКЛ. On and off.
Now go and look — with an adult, and without touching anything electrical. Generators, welders, pumps, old radios, medical equipment and machine tools are the places Cyrillic shows up.
Copy any Cyrillic you find, exactly, onto your paper. Sound out every word you copied.
If you find ОПАСНО anywhere, you have just read a genuine safety warning in Russian. Tell the adult with you what it means.
Bring your paper back and read your finds aloud to somebody.
modules.whyItWorks: Technical Russian is a small, repetitive vocabulary that appears on real objects, which makes it both learnable and immediately useful. Reading a genuine warning label is also the first time the language does a job for you rather than the other way round.
modules.challenge: Find Cyrillic on one piece of equipment near you and be the only person present who can read it.

modules.title: Capstone: The Scholarship Introduction
modules.bigIdea: Today you deliver, out loud and unscripted, the exact self-introduction a Russian university interviewer would ask you for.

seeThis.visual: Здравствуйте. Меня зовут… Я из… Я учу русский язык. Я хочу учиться в России.
seeThis.caption: Five sentences. This is genuinely what the opening of such an interview sounds like.

youNeed: a partner to play the interviewer
the phone once, to check stress
doThis: Write your own version of the five sentences with your real name and your real home.
Check every stress once against the audio, especially учиться — u-CHÍ-tsa — and Россия — ra-SSÍ-ya. Then put the phone away.
Stand up and say the whole thing five times without notes. Standing matters — it is how you will actually deliver it.
Now deliver it to a partner playing the interviewer, who shakes your hand and says Здравствуйте first. Do not break into another language at any point.
Write the full introduction in Cyrillic by hand on cardboard and hang it up. Every letter on it is one you decoded yourself over eight modules.
End with спасибо большое and a handshake.
modules.whyItWorks: This introduction is the single highest-value thing you can own in Russian, because it is both the interview opener and the way you will meet every Russian speaker for the rest of your life. Delivering it standing, live and unscripted is what makes it survive nerves.
modules.challenge: Deliver it to somebody who has actually studied in Russia, and ask them for one correction.

words.means: I want to study in Russia

courses.title: Arabic for Teens
courses.tagline: Three consonants make a root, and a root makes a whole family of words.
courses.intro: Arabic is built on three-letter roots. Take k-t-b and you get 'he wrote', 'book', 'office', 'library' and 'writer' — five words from one root, each with the same three letters sitting inside it. Learn to see the root and Arabic stops being a memory test and becomes a system. This course takes you from dots and joins to reading real signs and writing a real message.
courses.parentNote: Your teenager will finish able to read and write joined Arabic script, produce the difficult pharyngeal consonants, recognise the three-letter root system that underlies the whole language, read public signage, and write and speak a short real message. Arabic is an official language across North Africa, widely used in the Sahel and the Horn, one of the working languages of the African Union, and — where it matters to the family — the language of the Qur'an.

modules.title: The Dot Families
modules.bigIdea: Twenty-eight Arabic letters are built from far fewer shapes, and dots do most of the distinguishing work.

seeThis.visual: ب ت ث  ·  ج ح خ  ·  د ذ  ·  ر ز  ·  س ش
seeThis.caption: Five shapes, thirteen letters. In each family the skeleton is identical and only the dots move.

youNeed: chalk and a wall, or sand and a stick
doThis: Draw the boat shape and make all three of ب ت ث by moving the dots: one below, two above, three above.
Draw the hook shape and make ج ح خ: dot inside for j, no dot for ḥ, dot above for kh. The sounds are very different but the skeleton is one shape.
Draw the small hook for د and ذ, and the curve for ر and ز. In each pair, adding one dot above changes the sound.
Draw the three-tooth shape for س and add three dots above for ش.
Write all thirteen letters on your wall grouped in their families, with the family skeleton drawn once at the head of each row. Leave the chart up.
Explain your chart out loud to one person, family by family.
modules.whyItWorks: Grouping by skeleton means you learn five shapes instead of thirteen letters, and the dots become a small separate thing to remember rather than part of a new shape each time. This is one of the genuinely efficient routes into the Arabic alphabet.
modules.challenge: Draw a skeleton with no dots and have a friend add dots to make the letter you name. Ten rounds.

modules.title: Six Letters That Refuse to Hold Hands
modules.bigIdea: Arabic letters join to both sides — except six, which join only on the right, and those six are why words look like they have gaps.

seeThis.visual: ا د ذ ر ز و  ✋ | مدرسة  vs  دار
seeThis.caption: These six take a hand from the right but never give one to the left. That is what creates the breaks inside a word.

doThis: Write the six non-connectors big on one card: ا د ذ ر ز و. Say aloud: these six never join to the left.
Cut strips and build دار — dār — house — letter by letter, right to left. Notice د will not attach to the ا that follows it, so there is a visible gap.
Now build نور — nūr — light. The ن joins forward to the و, but the و stops dead and will not join the ر.
Copy all five words of this module by hand, joined, right to left, and circle every gap caused by a non-connector.
Write the six non-connectors on a card and stick it above where you write. You will check it constantly for a fortnight and then never again.
Read all five words aloud to somebody, pointing right to left and naming each gap you circled.
modules.whyItWorks: Gaps inside Arabic words confuse beginners badly, because they look like spaces between words. Knowing there are exactly six culprits turns an apparently chaotic feature into a short closed list, and reading speed jumps immediately.
modules.challenge: Write a friend's name in Arabic and challenge them to find where the gaps have to fall.

modules.title: Prices in the Souq
modules.bigIdea: Market Arabic is short, direct and identical from Nouakchott to Omdurman, and it is the fastest useful Arabic you can own.

seeThis.visual: بكم؟ 💰  غالي 😤  رخيص 🙂
seeThis.caption: How much? Expensive. Cheap. Three words and you can bargain.

youNeed: a friend to play the trader
doThis: Write each of the five words on a card, Arabic on the front, transliteration and meaning on the back.
Learn بكم — bikam — 'how much?' — as a single sound. Say it twenty times.
Set up a market. Your friend lays out five objects and names a price. You point at one and ask بكم؟
Reply with either غالي — ghālī — too expensive — or خذ — no, keep it simple — say طيب — ṭayyib — 'alright, good' — and take the item.
Swap roles and run the whole game again with silly prices so you use غالي often.
Write the full exchange out in joined Arabic on cardboard and hang it up.
modules.whyItWorks: Bargaining vocabulary is produced under mild social pressure, which is exactly the condition that makes language stick. It is also genuinely the first Arabic you will use if you ever travel north, so it earns its place ahead of prettier vocabulary.
modules.challenge: Run the market game with someone who does not speak Arabic and teach them their lines as you go.

modules.title: The Sounds Behind the Tongue
modules.bigIdea: Arabic has consonants made in the throat and the back of the mouth that no European language uses, and these are what mark out a real speaker.

seeThis.visual: ع ʿayn · ح ḥāʾ · خ khāʾ · ق qāf · ص ṣād
seeThis.caption: Five sounds from the back. Get ع and ح apart and everything else follows.

doThis: Listen to ع and ح side by side ten times before attempting either. They are made in the same place; ح is voiceless and breathy, ع is voiced and tight.
Hand on throat. Say ح — a hard whispered h with the throat narrowed. No buzz under your hand. Then ع — same narrowing, but now with voice, so you feel the buzz.
Now ق. Make a k as far back as you can, at the very root of the tongue, not where English k sits. Say قلب — qalb — heart — ten times.
Say ص in صديق — ṣadīq — friend. It is an s with the whole back of the tongue raised, giving it a dark, heavy sound.
Record yourself saying عربي, حياة, خير, قلب and صديق. Compare each with the model and rank them best to worst.
Re-record only your worst two until they are closer, then stop.
modules.whyItWorks: These consonants distinguish real words from each other, so getting them wrong changes meaning, not just accent. They also cannot be learned from any written description — the physical feedback of a hand on the throat plus a model voice is the only reliable route.
modules.challenge: Say ح and ع at a friend and ask which one they can feel a buzz in when they copy it.

modules.title: The Words of School and Scholarship
modules.bigIdea: Almost every word about learning in Arabic is built from a small number of roots, so the whole field arrives as one connected set.

seeThis.visual: مدرسة madrasa · طالب ṭālib · معلم muʿallim · جامعة jāmiʿa
seeThis.caption: School, student, teacher, university. The م prefix on several of them marks a place or a person.

doThis: Listen to the six words and repeat each five times, watching your ع in جامعة and معلم.
Notice the م at the front of مدرسة, معلم and مكتب. That prefix very often marks a place or the person who does something. Circle every م you see at the start of a word from now on.
Write مدرسة by hand ten times, joined, right to left. Then جامعة ten times.
Record yourself saying أنا طالب — anā ṭālib — 'I am a student'. Compare to the model.
Write أدرس اللغة العربية — adrusu al-lugha al-ʿarabiyya — 'I study the Arabic language' — on cardboard, joined, and hang it up.
Read that sentence aloud to one adult and tell them what it says.
modules.whyItWorks: Noticing the م prefix is your first look at Arabic's pattern system, and it arrives disguised as vocabulary. From here on, unfamiliar words start showing you clues about what kind of word they are before you know their meaning at all.
modules.challenge: Find three more Arabic words starting with م and guess whether each one is a place or a person. Then check.

modules.title: One Root, Five Words
modules.bigIdea: The three consonants k-t-b carry the idea of writing, and pouring them into different patterns produces an entire family of related words.

seeThis.visual: ك ت ب → كتب · كتاب · مكتب · مكتبة · كاتب
seeThis.caption: Look at each word and find the same three letters in the same order. They are always there.

doThis: Write the three root letters ك ت ب at the top of your paper. These three carry the meaning 'writing'.
Now write each of the five words below it, joined, and circle the ك, the ت and the ب inside every single one. They never move out of order.
Listen to all five on the phone and repeat each five times. Notice how the vowels between the root letters change while the consonants never do.
Look at the meanings: he wrote, book, office, library, writer. Every one is a different angle on the same idea.
Now predict. If م at the front often makes a place, and مكتب is an office, what would you guess مكتبة is? Check whether you were right.
Show your circled diagram to one person and explain the root system to them out loud.
modules.whyItWorks: The three-consonant root is the actual engine of Arabic, and seeing it once with your own pen through five real words explains more about the language than months of word lists. From here, new vocabulary arrives attached to words you already know rather than as separate items.
modules.challenge: Take the root د ر س (lesson, study) and see how many words you can find that contain it. مدرسة is one.

modules.title: Read the Signs on a Real Street
modules.bigIdea: Public Arabic signage uses a small closed vocabulary, and once you have it you can navigate a street in any Arabic-speaking city.

seeThis.visual: مدخل ⬅️ · خروج ➡️ · ممنوع 🚫 · مفتوح ✅ · مغلق ⛔
seeThis.caption: Entrance, exit, forbidden, open, closed. Note the م at the front of three of them.

youNeed: permission to walk with an adult
doThis: Learn the five words and write each one three times, joined, right to left.
Notice ممنوع — mamnūʿ — forbidden — has your م prefix and your ع from module 4. You can now read it from parts you already know.
Go out with an adult and look for Arabic on shopfronts, mosque noticeboards, imported packaging, medicine boxes and any signage near you.
Copy every piece of Arabic you find, exactly, joined, right to left.
Sound out each one aloud. For any word you cannot read, circle the letters you DO recognise. That partial reading is real progress.
Make five cards with the sign words and put them on the right doors in your own home. Leave them there.
modules.whyItWorks: Sign vocabulary repeats constantly and is written in large clear type, making it the ideal first real reading material. Partial decoding — recognising some letters in an unknown word — is also exactly what a developing reader does, and practising it deliberately speeds everything up.
modules.challenge: Find one piece of Arabic writing nobody else nearby can read, and read it to them.

modules.title: Capstone: Write and Speak a Real Message
modules.bigIdea: Today you write a short message in your own hand in Arabic script and deliver a full spoken introduction to a real person.

seeThis.visual: أهلا وسهلا. اسمي… أنا من… أدرس اللغة العربية. شكرا جزيلا.
seeThis.caption: Read right to left. Five lines: a real greeting, your name, your home, what you are doing, and thanks.

youNeed: paper or cardboard and a pen
the phone once, to check pronunciation
doThis: Write your own five lines out by hand, joined, right to left, with your real name and your real home. Take your time with the joins — this is the piece of work the whole course was building towards.
Check every ع, ح and ق once against the audio, then put the phone away.
Stand up and say all five lines aloud five times without looking at your paper.
Deliver the introduction to a real person, face to face. Greet with أهلا وسهلا, run all five lines, and do not switch languages.
Hand them the paper you wrote by hand. Let them look at it while you read it aloud, pointing right to left.
Finish with شكرا جزيلا and مع السلامة.
modules.whyItWorks: Writing by hand and speaking aloud in the same session uses two different memory systems on the same content, which is why the pairing holds so well. Handing somebody something you wrote in a script you could not read eight modules ago is also the clearest possible evidence of what you have done.
modules.challenge: Give your handwritten message to someone who reads Arabic and ask them for exactly one correction to your handwriting.
